activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Bentley had been setting up the hanukkiah on the kitchen windowsill when the doorbell rang, and now Shanaya was standing in the hallway with her boots still on, holding a plate of her mother's biscotti. "My mom said to bring these," she said. "Also, I have a question, and it's been bugging me since class on Monday."

"Ask it after the candles," Bentley's father called from the stove, where the latkes were frying.

"No, now," Shanaya said. She pointed at the menorah. "Hanukkah is eight nights, right? We learned that. So why does that thing have nine spots for candles?"

Bentley looked at the hanukkiah. He counted the branches with his eyes, touching each one with a fingertip. Eight across, in two rows of four, and one taller branch standing apart in the middle. Nine. He had lit it every year of his life, and he had never once counted. "Huh," he said.

"Don't ask me," his father said, flipping a latke. "You're the one who wants to be an engineer. Figure it out."

Bentley picked up a box of candles and tipped them out onto the table. He placed one candle in each of the eight lower branches, then held up the ninth. Shanaya watched him with her arms crossed, waiting. He looked at the tall middle branch, then at the candles in his hand, and then at the box, where the word shamash was printed in small letters beside a picture of a single candle set slightly apart from the rest. "Shamash," he said slowly, reading it. "I've heard my grandma say that word. It's the helper candle." He set the ninth candle in the tall branch. "Eight for the eight nights," he said, "and this one lights the others. That's why it's taller. So you can tell it apart."

"So you'd never light the eight with a match?" Shanaya asked.

Bentley realized he had never actually watched closely enough to know. He had always been busy holding the door open or fetching his little cousins. "Let's find out," he said. "Tonight's the fourth night, so we do four plus the shamash."

When his father finally turned off the stove, the whole family crowded into the kitchen. Bentley's grandmother struck the match and touched it only to the shamash, then lifted the shamash out of its branch and carried its flame to the first candle, then the second, then the third, then the fourth, chanting the blessing while the flames wobbled. Shanaya leaned in beside Bentley, close enough that he could hear her breathing. The candles guttered and steadied, and the oil smell from the latkes condensed on the cold window above them into a faint fog.

After the blessings, the adults drifted back to the table for dinner, but Bentley and Shanaya stayed by the window, watching the flames. Steam condensed on his juice glass, too, and he drew a crooked star in it with his thumbnail. "It's cumulative," Shanaya said. "Like, every night you add one more, so by the last night the whole thing is lit, all eight plus the helper."

"That's kind of the point, I think," Bentley said. "It gets brighter the whole way through."

"I like that," Shanaya said. She picked up a biscotti and pointed it at the hanukkiah like a baton. "Same time tomorrow? I want to see the fifth one."

"Bring more of these," Bentley said, and took one for himself.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
story:
Justin had never built a spreadsheet before, and the empty grid on Mr. Ramírez's classroom computer looked like a piece of graph paper waiting to embarrass him. The tech club was keeping score for the sixth-grade reading challenge, and whoever built the tracker got to present it at Friday assembly. Justin wanted that job. He typed each class's book count into a column, then hunted through the menus until he found SUM and dragged it across the cells. A total appeared at the bottom, and he leaned back so fast his chair squeaked.

Then Quinn leaned over his shoulder. "That total's wrong. Room 12 read 43 books, not 34. You flipped the digits." Justin checked her list and groaned. He clicked on the cell with 34, typed 43 instead, and before he touched anything else, the grand total at the bottom changed on its own. He stared at it. He changed the number back to 34, watched the total drop, then typed 43 again and watched it climb right back. "It's watching the whole column," he said slowly. "Change anything inside it and the total fixes itself."

He had to be sure. He picked a harmless cell at the top, added ten to it, and the total went up by exactly ten the instant he pressed enter. He put it back. Myah, who was building the chart next to him, had been quiet this whole time, the way she got when she was concentrating. "Make the bars now," she said. "The chart reads the same numbers, so it should follow them too." Justin highlighted the column and inserted a bar chart, and five bars jumped onto the screen, the tallest one belonging to Room 9.

That night he couldn't stop thinking about it, so he texted Quinn. "I fixed the typo and the total changed before I even asked it to. SUM watches the range." Her reply came fast. "So if Mr. Ramírez adds books tomorrow, the chart updates too?" He wrote back, "Try it. Change one cell, watch the bar." In the morning, sunlight through the window refracted off the screen while Quinn tapped in a new number, and the bar for her class grew taller without either of them touching the chart.

At Friday assembly, Justin stood in front of everyone with the projector glowing behind him. "One typo taught me the best part," he said. "Fix the number, and the total and the chart fix themselves." Afterward Myah nudged him. "Told you typing stamina pays off." Justin laughed and said, "Mistakes are inevitable. Fixing them is automatic."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
story:
"Two hundred and sixty dollars," Bennett read off the price tag, and Remi groaned so loudly that a shopper two racks away turned to look. They were standing outside the glass case at the mall's sneaker store, where the new purple-and-gray Hyperglides sat in a floodlit display. Two weeks ago, the same shoes had been one hundred and eighty dollars, and Bennett had been saving toward them ever since he saw the first leaked photo online.

"That's robbery," said Remi, fogging the glass with his breath. A sales clerk unlocked the case for a boy ahead of them, and Bennett noticed the shelf behind it was nearly bare, just three boxes left in the whole row. Meanwhile, across the aisle, a mountain of last year's model sat under a giant orange sign shouting 40% OFF, and nobody was even looking at it. Bennett felt something click, the way it did in math class when a hard problem suddenly made sense. Scarce and wanted meant expensive. Plentiful and ignored meant cheap. He said it out loud, and Remi nodded slowly, like it was a secret code they had just cracked.

They tested it on the way to the food court. The limited-edition boba flavor, the one the shop had announced would only run for a month, cost six dollars and had a line out the door. Regular lemonade was a dollar fifty and the pitcher looked big enough to swim in. "Pattern confirmed," Bennett said, holding up his cup like a trophy.

At the pickup loop outside, Bennett's mom was idling in the car, and Brinley from his science class was leaning out of her family's minivan at the gas pump next to it. "Hey, Bennett!" she called over. "You know anything about gas? It was way cheaper last week and my dad's all grumpy about it." Bennett thought about his sneaker rule for a second, then remembered what his mom had said in the car that morning, complaining into her opaque sunglasses that the biggest single chunk of what you pay for a gallon is the cost of the crude oil itself, so when crude goes up, pump prices climb right along with it. "The crude oil," he called back. "It's the biggest part of the price, so when it rises, the pump price rises too." Brinley repeated it to her dad, who gave a thumbs-up out the window like Bennett had won him a prize.

In the car, Bennett told his mom about the sneakers, the boba, and Brinley's question, all in one breathless rush. She laughed and said his voice could irritate a librarian at fifty paces when he got this excited. Bennett didn't care. He had a plan: he would ride out the sneaker hype, wait for the price to plateau somewhere reasonable, and then, with any luck, swoop in with his saved allowance. He turned to watch the mall shrink in the side mirror, its glass doors flashing in the sun. "Next month, Hyperglides," he said. "Next month they're mine."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Jake sat on the living room rug with his grandfather's old keyboard propped against the couch, because choosing the drums last fall had been a mistake he was still hearing about at dinner. "You quit piano at eight," his mom kept saying, "so why would drums be different?" He hadn't answered then, but he had an answer now: this time he wanted it. The problem was the sheet music. His song had a swirl at the start of every line, and the notes floated like stars with no map.

He texted a picture of the page to Mohamed-Amine, who had been playing since second grade. "What's the swirly thing?" he typed. Three dots blinked for a long time. "It's also called the G clef," Mohamed-Amine wrote back. "That's all I'm telling you. Figure out the rest, detective."

G clef. Jake stared at the swirl until his eyes watered. If the symbol had a note's name attached to it, maybe the swirl was pointing at something, the way a hitchhiker's thumb points at a road. He grabbed a pencil and traced the curl slowly, the graphite squeaking against the page. The swirl looped around and around, and there, on the second line up from the bottom, it circled one line like a lasso catching a fence post. He counted the lines from the bottom: one, two. He played the key he thought was that G, then played the note written on that line in his song. Same sound. His ears did a little jump. The curl circles the staff line for G. It wasn't decoration, it was an address.

"Elie, guess what," he said at school the next morning, holding up his messy pencil page. Elie squinted at it. "That page is deteriorating fast," he said. "You traced that thing about fifty times." Jake tapped the circled line. "Second line is G. The whole swirl wraps around it. I checked on the keyboard and everything." Elie played clarinet and had his own opinions. "Prove it," he said, so at lunch they huddled over Elie's music in the cafeteria, and the proof worked there too, on a page Jake had never seen.

The real verdict came that Thursday, when Ms. Guo, the neighbour who taught piano across the hall, knocked to complain about the same four measures played sixty times. Jake showed her his pencil tracing instead of apologizing. She looked at it, then at him, and a small smile crept onto her face. "You found the trick on your own," she said. "Most students just memorize it and forget."

That evening the living room sounded different. The notes on the second line came out confident and round, and the rest of the song organized itself around them like houses around a lamppost. His fingers still stumbled, and the old keyboard's middle speaker buzzed on anything above E, but the page was no longer barren, every black dot had a place to live. He set his pencil down on the second line, right in the heart of the curl, and played the whole first line without stopping.

story:
Hailey slid her worksheet across the table so Chiara could see it. "Every other problem gave me a number at the end. This one just says two equals two."

Chiara leaned over the equation, 2x + 2 = 2(x + 1), and frowned. "That can't be right. Something must have gone wrong."

At the front of the math club room, Mr. Okonkwo was handing out challenge problems for the tournament in two weeks, and Hailey wanted one of the top three spots badly. She had stayed up late practicing, and now the whole page depended on a problem that seemed to dissolve in her hands. First she had subtracted 2 from both sides, then divided, and the x had simply vanished, like a magician's scarf pulled through a fist. She winced and erased her last step, wondering if she'd broken some rule without noticing.

"Test it," she said, mostly to herself. "If x is one, the left side is four, and the right side is two times two, so four. If x is ten, the left side is twenty-two, and the right side is two times eleven." She tried zero, then a negative number, writing fast. Every time, the two sides came out equal. "It works for every number I pick."

"Then what's the answer?" Chiara asked.

"There isn't one answer. Every number works." Hailey stared at the two lines on the page. "They're the same expression, just written differently. It's like if I called myself Hailey and someone else called me by my middle name. Still me."

Steve dropped into the chair beside them, peering at her paper. "Two equals two? Did your intestine twist halfway through?" He laughed at his own joke, but Hailey barely heard it, because she was already flipping back through her notes to the other problems. Those had given answers like x = 5 because the two sides were genuinely different, and only one number could make them match. This one was different.

When Mr. Okonkwo reached their table, Hailey raised her hand. "For this problem, every number works, because both sides are the same expression written differently."

"Correct," he said, and moved her worksheet to the small stack marked "Advanced." The stack for people going to the tournament.

Chiara nudged her. "Told you nothing went wrong."

Hailey pulled the next problem toward her, clicked her pencil, and started in on the left side.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
story:
Leo had signed up to volunteer at the community food bank that operated out of the annex behind the animal shelter, mostly because his mother had said he needed to do something useful over spring break. He had expected the place to smell like kibble, since the dogs were right through the connecting door, but the annex smelled like oranges. Three crates of oranges, a bin of lettuce with brown edges, and a shelf of dented canned soup covered most of the floor.

"Grocery store donations," said Kayson, who had been volunteering there since January and clearly considered himself an expert. "We sort the good from the bad, box up the good, and Mr. Oliveira takes whatever people won't eat over to the animals. Pigs get a lot of it."

Leo picked up a bag of grapes with one squashed bunch at the bottom. "So this whole bag counts as bad because of one bunch?" he asked.

"That's the rule."

That seemed bizarre to Leo. He pulled the squashed bunch out, set it aside, and looked at the rest of the grapes, which were fine. If stores threw away whole bags because of one bad part, no wonder there was so much food here. He started keeping count on the back of a receipt, one tally for every container where only part of the food was spoiled. By the time he hit nineteen, only four containers were spoiled all the way through.

"I hypothesize the store just doesn't want to pay someone to pick through it," Leo said, tapping the receipt. "It's faster to toss the whole thing."

"You hypothesize?" Kayson said, grinning. "You sound like my science teacher." But he came over and looked at the tallies anyway. On the wall by the sink there was a poster with smiling vegetables on it, and Kayson read the small print out loud. "The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted." He whistled. "Thirty to 40 percent. That's almost half."

Leo stared at his tally sheet. Part of that number had to be bags like this, whole containers tossed for one soft bunch. He tested his idea on the next crate of lettuce. Instead of throwing the brown-edged bin out, he stripped the outer leaves off each head and put the pale green centers in the people box. He got eight good heads out of it, enough for eight families.

Mr. Oliveira came through the connecting door with an empty wheelbarrow, looked at the two boxes, and raised an eyebrow at the tallies on the receipt. "You want to write down the numbers every week? If we can show the store how much is still good, maybe they'll sort it before it comes to us." He slid the wheelbarrow over for the outer leaves and the squashed grapes, which the pigs apparently would not mind at all.

Leo said yes before he finished thinking about it. That night he sat at the kitchen table trying to finish an English assignment, a poem about his week, and found himself writing a stanza about oranges and lettuce heads and the smell of dogs through a doorway. He read it once, crossed out two lines, and wrote a better one underneath.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
story:
The bus home from school smelled like wet boots and oranges, and Evan had his laptop balanced on his knees, flipping between two baseball pages. He wanted to settle an argument with Hendrik once and for all: which player was better, David Justice or Derek Jeter, back in the nineties? He had the numbers, and numbers didn't lie.

"Look," Evan said, turning the screen toward Audrey, who slid into the seat across the aisle. "In 1995, Justice had a higher batting average than Jeter. And in 1996, Justice beat him again. Two years, two wins. Hendrik owes me a pop."

Audrey leaned in, chewing the end of her pencil. "Show me 1996." She squinted. "Okay, yeah. Justice, higher. Both years." She sat back, looking vaguely ominous, like a math teacher about to hand back a test nobody passed. "So case closed."

Evan grinned and started typing, planning to add the two seasons together for a victory chart, the kind with bars. He was already imagining the picture he'd text to Hendrik. Then he stopped typing. He ran the addition again. He ran it a third time, because the screen was telling him something that couldn't be true: Jeter's average for the two years combined was higher than Justice's.

"That's broken," Evan said. "The site's broken."

"It's two sites," Audrey said, pulling out her phone to check a different one. A minute later she held it up. "Same thing."

A kid a few rows back yelled something about a snow day, and the driver's wipers squeaked against the drizzle, but Evan barely heard any of it. He stared at the numbers. Justice won 1995. Justice won 1996. Put the seasons together and Jeter won. It felt like a magic trick with no magician in sight. Somewhere in his head, an idea began to germinate: maybe combining years wasn't the same as adding up wins, maybe the seasons themselves were doing something he couldn't see from the two averages alone. He grabbed a napkin from his lunch bag and started copying figures, testing one small idea after another, crossing most of them out.

"You realize," Audrey said, watching him scribble through a pothole, "that you can't actually send Hendrik a victory chart now."

Evan laughed, though it stung a little. That was the irony of the whole afternoon: he'd gone hunting for proof he was right and come home with proof the question was wrong. "I'm sending him this instead," he said. "Both seasons and the combined one. Let him lose sleep over it."

The bus lurched around the corner by the corner store, and Evan slid the napkin into his binder, careful not to smudge it. "First one to figure out why it works buys the pop," he said.

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
story:
Grace counted the survey rows for the third time and got a different answer again. Two hundred and six students had answered the question "Should the cafeteria serve tacos every week?" and Ms. Patel wanted the results summarized by grade before Friday's assembly. Grace had been highlighting rows and tallying by hand, and every tally came out different.

"You're going to wear a hole in that trackpad," said Louie, leaning over from the next computer. "My dad says nobody does it this way anymore. At his office they use something called a pivot table."

"A what?"

"A pivot table. That's the actual name. He says a guy named Pito Salas invented it, back when he was working on a spreadsheet program called Lotus Improv. It came out in 1991." Louie shrugged. "He got all excited telling me. Said his colleagues still cherish the day they learned it, because it turned a whole afternoon of counting into two minutes."

Grace opened the help menu and found the pivot table option, half hidden under a menu she had never clicked. She dragged the grade field into the rows box and the taco answer into the values box, then hit refresh. The spreadsheet reorganized itself instantly: grade six, forty-one yes; grade seven, fifty-three yes; grade eight, thirty-eight yes. The rest were no votes, split neatly by row.

"Wait," said Akram from across the lab, wheeling his chair over. "Why does grade eight have so many more no votes than the others? Last year grade eight was the grade that petitioned for pizza Fridays." Grace stared at the numbers. She remembered that the grade eight survey had gone out the same week the cafeteria had raised prices, right when everyone was annoyed about everything. Maybe the tacos weren't really the issue. She wondered if the results were biased by timing, so she ran a filter to see which day each grade's answers had come in, and sure enough, most of the grade eight no votes were from the price-hike week. She tested it by separating the answers into two pivot tables, one for each week, and in the second week grade eight flipped to mostly yes.

Ms. Patel walked the aisle, stopped behind Grace's screen, and read the two tables side by side. "So what do we tell the assembly?"

Grace highlighted the second table. "Tell them tacos won. But if anyone asks why the first week looked weird, blame the price hike, not the tacos."

story:
Dylan had promised Mr. Yip a poster for the community centre's heritage night, a big pie chart of the origins of people in a small town in Manitoba. He had the numbers from a census website, and they were broken. Scottish, 34 percent. Ukrainian, 22. English, 19. German, 12. Filipino, 11. He added them twice on the whiteboard in the craft room and got 98 percent both times, which was fine. Then he noticed he'd skipped a line. With the last two entries included, the total was 127 percent.

"You drew the pie wrong," said Vivienne, looking over his shoulder. "Or the town's impossible. One of those."

"It's not my pie," Dylan said. He drew a circle on the whiteboard and tried to decompose it into wedges that added up to more than the whole thing. It couldn't be done. A circle was a circle. Unless the wedges overlapped, which pies, in his experience, did not do.

Lina arrived with the glue gun and took the defiant view that the website was simply lying to them, the way websites did. She suggested he cut the extra 27 percent and go home. Dylan instead went to the computer room and searched until he found a page about the census. He read one line out loud, slowly, like a person checking a receipt: "The census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population."

Vivienne frowned. "Since 1981? That's, what, before my dad was even bald."

"So a person can be Scottish and Ukrainian at the same time," Dylan said. He wrote it on the whiteboard and drew two overlapping circles, like a Venn diagram, which was not a pie at all. "The wedges overlap. That's why it's over a hundred." He felt the particular joy of a rule discovered rather than told, and then the particular deflation of a poster to redo.

He stayed late, cutting new shapes. Instead of a pie he built overlapping circles with the community centre'spopulation written along the bottom, and in each overlap he taped a small photo of a real person from the centre. Mrs. Ocampo in the Filipino-Ukrainian overlap. The twins from swim practice in three circles at once. Mr. Yip came in at the end, looked at the poster for a long moment, and said, "So who's the antagonist here, the pie chart or the census?"

"The pie chart," Dylan said. "It started the fight."

story:
Scarlett arrived at the community centre with a roll of paper under her arm and a deadline hanging over her. Malaya's sign-language club met in the craft room every Saturday, and tonight was their open house, which meant the poster had to be finished before the first families walked through the doors at seven. She spread the paper across two pushed-together tables and uncapped the markers. The headline was the problem. She had written DEAF CLUB in tall blue letters, and something about it nagged at her.

"That's not how we write it," Malaya said, hands moving as she spoke, the way she always talked at the centre where half the room signed anyway. She tapped the first letter. "Capital D. One word, two meanings."

"Since when does deaf get a capital letter?" Scarlett said. "It's not a name."

Malaya pulled a worn book from her bag, a memoir by a Deaf writer, and flipped to the flyleaf where she had pencilled a note. "In 1972, James Woodward proposed writing Deaf with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users. Lowercase deaf is just the hearing condition itself." She set the book down. "Small d is the ear. Big D is us."

Scarlett looked at the wall of posters from other clubs. The knitting circle had knitted its letters. The nocturnal wildlife club, which met here on Thursday nights to listen for owls, had painted a moon. Nobody else's poster had a hidden rule inside it. She tested the idea in her head: her own grandmother had a deaf ear from a childhood fever, but her grandmother wasn't in a signing community, so she would be lowercase. Malaya's whole family signed at the dinner table, laughing and arguing with their hands flying. Big D. The pattern held. She erased the small d and drew a taller one, then painted the D three times the size of the rest, red, with a pair of hands signing underneath it.

The room began to fill. Ms. Fitzgerald, who taught the cooking class down the hall and knew more about this centre than anyone, stopped in front of the poster. Scarlett braced herself, suddenly worried she had made it worse, that she had embarrassed herself in front of the whole club by guessing at a rule she'd only just learned.

Ms. Fitzgerald studied it, then lifted her hands and signed something quick. Malaya laughed and translated. "She says she'll trade you a poster for a poster. She wants one for her class."

"For cooking?"

"For her Deaf seniors' coffee morning. Thursdays." Ms. Fitzgerald pulled out her phone and showed a photo of her own group, ten people signing over a tray of scones. "They've been meeting here for years," Malaya interpreted, "and nobody ever made them a poster."

Scarlett looked at her roll of paper, half of it still unused. "Tell her Thursday's my night off. I'll be here." Ms. Fitzgerald grinned and signed one more word, slow enough that even Scarlett recognized it. Thank you.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
story:
Charlie stood on the polished gym floor with her sneakers squeaking, dreading the moment Ms. Greco would pair them up. She had signed up for the improv workshop because Maryam begged her to, and now Maryam was laughing with Matthieu across the circle like this was easy.

"Today we learn partnering," Ms. Greco said. She held up a battered paperback with a cracked spine, its cover soft from handling. "This book started it all. Viola Spolin collected theater games in 1963, and people still call it the bible of improv teaching. But you can't read your way into improv. You have to do it."

She explained the game in one breath: your partner makes an offer, a line, a gesture, anything, and you accept it with "yes, and," then build on it. Matthieu went first with Maryam and knocked it out in three lines, pirates on a sinking raft, and everyone clapped. Then Ms. Greco pointed at Charlie.

Her partner was Matthieu, of course, because the universe was like that. He stepped in front of her and said, "We're trapped in this gym and the doors are melting."

Charlie's instinct was to say, that's silly, doors don't melt. She could feel the word "no" rising like a reflex. Then she thought about what had actually just happened with Matthieu and Maryam, and it wasn't the pirate raft that made the scene work. It was that neither of them pushed back. There was an invisible rule underneath the game, something you couldn't see, only test. So she tested it.

"Yes, and I found a bucket of ice behind the bleachers," she said, and pointed.

"Yes, and the bucket is full of frozen sandwiches," Matthieu said, eyes lighting up.

"Yes, and we have to feed them to the melting doors before lunch."

The circle was laughing now, and Ms. Greco was writing something on her clipboard, and Charlie realized she had stopped planning two lines ahead and was just falling forward, word after word, like stepping stones she laid only after her foot was already in the air. She decided to invest her whole attention in Matthieu's next offer instead of her own fear, and it worked, the way it always seemed to work for Maryam.

Afterward, while everyone else stacked the mats, Charlie drifted toward the bench where Ms. Greco had left the old paperback. She picked it up, and a folded page slipped out from between chapter markers, a page of penciled notes in slanted handwriting she recognized. It was her mother's handwriting, from her college drama binder, on a photocopy of the same book.

"Ms. Greco," Charlie said slowly, "did you know my mom?"

Ms. Greco smiled like sunlight through a prism, splitting into something luminous and surprised. "I lent her this book twenty years ago. She never returned it." She tapped the cover. "I only got it back last month."

Charlie looked down at the soft, worn pages, at the ghost of her mother's pencil marks, and hugged the book to her chest without meaning to.

"You can borrow it," Ms. Greco said. "But this time, it comes back."

story:
Abigail had agreed to babysit for one evening at her cousin Theo's house, watching the little girl who lived next door while both sets of parents attended the same wedding reception. The girl was two, her name was Maren, and she was asleep before eight. It seemed almost too easy. Theo had left a note on the counter: snacks in the fridge, Wi-Fi password on the back, and if anything goes wrong, call my mom. That last part felt slightly arbitrary, since Theo's mom would be unreachable in a loud reception hall, but Abigail didn't argue with a note.

Around nine, a sound from the hallway made her look up from her homework. Maren was supposed to be in the crib. She was not in the crib. Abigail found her standing at the end of the kitchen, holding a spray bottle almost as tall as her torso, and the cap was off, and there was a wet stripe across the floor where she had dragged it. Abigail's heart did something she felt in her throat. She knelt down and took the bottle gently, the way she'd take a crayon from a dog, and checked Maren's mouth, her hands, the front of her pajamas. Drool, no smell of cleaner, no blue lips. But two-year-olds were fast, and Abigail had been reading a textbook for twenty minutes.

She could not see what had happened in the past. That was the problem. The evidence was a wet floor and a toddler who seemed fine, which could mean nothing or could mean something that hadn't started yet. She remembered her mother saying once that you shouldn't guess in situations like this, and that hospitals were not always the answer either. Then she looked at the fridge, where Theo's family kept a strip of taped paper with emergency numbers, and among them, one unfamiliar line: Poison Help, 1-800-222-1222.

She called it, holding Maren on her hip. A woman answered on the second ring, even though it was past nine on a Saturday, and she didn't sound tired at all. "Poison control," she said, "this is the local center. What happened?"

Abigail explained about the bottle and the cap and the wet floor, and the woman asked careful questions. What was the product name? Had Maren vomited or coughed? Abigail read the label, which the woman said was a good sign, since she'd need it. "Most of these floor sprays just upset the stomach if any is swallowed," the woman said, "but stay on the line with me and keep an eye on her for the next hour." She stayed on the line, walked Abigail through what to watch for, and told her to call back at any hour if anything changed, because someone would always pick up.

Maren fell asleep again at ten, unharmed, one sock missing, completely indifferent to the alarm she had caused. Abigail sat beside the crib with her phone in her lap and the number copied into her contacts. When Theo's mom finally texted to ask how it went, Abigail typed back a single line: "Fine. Your fridge number is a lifesaver." Then she reached over and pulled the blanket up over Maren's bare foot.

Thomas had spent three days eating lunch at the far end of the cafeteria, and he could infer exactly why Wali kept choosing the table near the windows: it was the one spot where he never had to look at Thomas. All of this had started because Angel had asked Thomas to help with the science fair project on Friday, the same Friday as Wali's birthday sleepover, and Thomas had picked Angel. Today, though, Thomas came armed. He had a battered notebook from Ms. Morin's class, open to a page headed with two names: Carl Rogers and Richard Farson. They were the psychologists who introduced the term "active listening" back in 1957, which basically meant that when someone talked, you tried to understand their point of view, and you proved it by repeating their meaning back in your own words. Ms. Morin had made the whole class practice it, and Thomas had thought it was the most boring hour of his life until this week, when he decided it might be the only thing that could save him.

He slid his tray down across from Wali, who stared at his mashed potatoes like they were the last food on Earth.

"You can't sit there," Wali said.

"I can, actually. There's no law." Thomas set down the notebook anyway. "Also, I'm sorry. And before you yell, I'm going to try something radical. I'm going to listen instead of talking."

"That would be a first."

Wali complained for a while, mostly about the group chat, and Thomas held on to every word the way he held on to facts about beetles, which was to say obsessively. When Wali finally paused, Thomas took a breath. "So you felt I picked her over you? Like Angel mattered more, without me even asking?"

Wali's shoulders dropped about an inch. He looked genuinely startled, like a larva that had just realized it had wings coming. "Yeah," he said. "That's it exactly. Huh."

Angel appeared behind them with her tray and a grin. "Are you two doing the Rogers and Farson thing? Ms. Morin has that same page taped inside her desk, you know. She calls it her emergency friendship repair manual."

"It's not a repair manual," Thomas said. "It's a technique from 1957. Very scientific."

"It's you saying one sentence that isn't about yourself," Wali said, but he was smiling now, which was the first time in three days. He tore his cookie in half and pushed the bigger piece across the table. "You're still buying me a slice of pizza for the sleepover I missed having you at."

"Two slices," Thomas said, "and I get to keep the notebook page."

"Deal," said Wali, and Angel stole the cookie half while they shook on it.

story:
On Tuesday the rumor about Billie's muddy shoes started to circulate through the seventh-grade hallway, and by lunch it had grown teeth. "Billie stepped in the port-a-potty puddle," someone announced near the vending machines, and a knot of kids laughed so hard one of them snorted milk. Jonathan gripped his tray and looked over at Billie, who was pretending to be fascinated by the cafeteria's tedious poster about recycling, the one with the smiling cartoon bottle.

The teaser was a big kid from math class, and Jonathan's heart hammered like a drum line. Katie nudged him. "Say something," she whispered. So Jonathan did what felt natural and awesome in his head. "At least Billie's shoes are cleaner than your grades," he fired back. The big kid blinked, then grinned, and the whole table exploded. Now they were teasing Billie and Jonathan, loudly, and the milk-snorting kid started a chant. Billie slid lower in his seat. Jonathan's great comeback had poured gasoline on everything.

In Mr. Adeyemi's science class that afternoon, Jonathan stared at the diagram of a network of circuits and had a weird thought. When someone insults you and you insult back, you're handing them fresh wires to connect to. They take your words and build on them. What if you gave them nothing to build with? He tested the idea in his head all through a lecture so tedious he could hear the clock ticking, and by the last bell he had a plan, which felt enormous, like discovering a secret trapdoor.

Wednesday at lunch, the teaser strolled over and said, "How's the toilet shoes kid doing today?" The cafeteria went quiet in that electric way. Jonathan set down his fork, kept his voice level, and said, "That's not funny. Stop." Four words, calm as a substitute teacher taking attendance. The big kid waited for a comeback, and Jonathan offered nothing else, just picked up his fork and kept eating. The silence stretched. The milk kid looked around for material and found none. The big kid muttered something and drifted back to his table, and the chant never happened.

Billie slid his tray over and said, "That was the smoothest thing I've ever seen. Teach me." Katie raised her juice box like a toast. Jonathan grinned so wide his cheeks hurt, and the smell of tater tots suddenly seemed like the best smell in the world.

"Same time tomorrow," Jonathan said, and pulled out a napkin to draw his first lesson plan.

story:
Isla spread the printed climate graphs across her grandfather's kitchen table, between his teacup and a puzzle with three missing edge pieces. Her homework said to compare a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature, and Ms. MacLeod had added one line at the bottom in red pen: check the rule before you decide what you have.

The graphs came from an anonymous climate database online, which felt to Isla like being handed evidence by someone wearing a paper bag over their head. Still, the numbers were the numbers. One graph showed a desert city where the temperature bar climbed high all year but the rainfall bars were nearly invisible, like someone had started drawing them and given up. The other, labeled as a rainforest, had rainfall bars so tall they ran into each other, and a temperature line that barely bothered to move.

She remembered sitting at this same table two summers ago, stuck on a math worksheet, when her grandfather had told her about his first flat and the landlord who insisted the damp patch on the ceiling was "character." He had put a glass under the drip every night for a week and lined the glasses up on the counter. Numbers, he'd said, are just glasses under a drip. You count them, and then the ceiling has to admit what it's doing.

So she counted. The rainforest graph had twelve months, and she went down the rainfall column with her pencil. January, 90 millimeters. February, 110. March, 95. Every single month cleared 60. Then the temperature column, and every month sat at 18 degrees Celsius or higher, most of them well above. That was the rule her notes stated: in the Koppen climate system, a tropical rainforest climate has every month averaging at least 18 degrees Celsius and at least 60 millimeters of rain. Every month. Not most months.

"Koppen," she said aloud, mostly to the teacup. "That's the name for it. Koppen."

Her grandfather looked up from the puzzle. "Bless you."

She texted Raya: is it still rainforest if ONE month dips below 60? Raya replied with a screenshot of a graph where November showed 55 millimeters, from Cassandra's set. Isla wrote back: no. one month under 60 and it's not. she has to pick a different city.

Raya sent back a single exclamation point, which for Raya was practically an essay. Isla could picture Cassandra trying to refute her with that graph anyway, holding it up in class, and she wanted to be there when Ms. MacLeod leaned in and read the November bar out loud.

She pulled the desert graph closer and wrote her first comparison sentence. Then she set her pencil down, went to the cupboard, found a glass, and placed it upside down over the missing puzzle pieces, like a tiny museum exhibit.

"That's for later," she told her grandfather, and went back to counting.

story:
The printer at Grandma's house made a sound like a cat coughing, and Alexandra leaned over it, waiting. She had found the charter on her laptop, but Grandma insisted paper was better for studying. "You can carry paper to the porch," Grandma had said, and now Alexandra's one-page copy sat diagonal across the tray, ink still wet, listing the freedoms her teacher expected her to explain in her own words by Monday.

Her phone buzzed. Drew. The city was closing Miller Park, the only one close enough to walk to, and Drew wanted to organize a protest at Monday's council meeting. Curtis thought a protest might get them all in trouble. "Meet me at Grandma's," Alexandra typed. "Bring Curtis." She had a feeling, half a hunch, that the answer to their argument was on the page in her hand, if she could only read it carefully enough.

When they arrived, Grandma served lemonade and then left them to it, humming in the kitchen. Curtis dropped into the wicker chair. "So we do nothing?"

Alexandra spread the page flat. "I have to explain one of these rights for class anyway, so let's actually check." She ran her finger down the sections. Section 2 caught her eye, and she read it aloud, slowly, the way Grandma had taught her to read anything important. "Section 2 of the Canadian Charter protects fundamental freedoms. Freedom of religion. Freedom of expression. Freedom of peaceful assembly." She paused on the last word. "And freedom of association."

"Peaceful assembly," Curtis repeated. "That's a gathering. Like ours." He leaned in, and Alexandra watched his expression shift as he connected it to his uncle's story, testing the idea against what he remembered. "My uncle's group blocked a road. That's why they got moved along. It wasn't peaceful assembly. It was something else." Drew grabbed a napkin and began printing the four freedoms in block letters, planning a sign that would name Section 2 outright, so nobody could claim they didn't know the law.

"Can I come with you Monday?" Curtis asked. "I want to stand with you. Empathy, right? After what happened to my uncle." Alexandra said he could accompany them, and Grandma, who had been listening from the doorway without any of them noticing, set down a plate of oatmeal cookies and picked up the page. She read it twice, then pointed at the words peaceful assembly and said, "Now say it in your own words, dear. That's the assignment."

Alexandra took a breath. "It means we're allowed to stand together in public, quietly, to say what we think, and the law calls that a fundamental freedom."

"Write that on the sign too," said Drew, and held out the marker.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
story:
Ellie sat on the low concrete wall at the skate park, her left arm resting in a bright green cast, watching Enzo grind the rail for the fourth time. She had been off her board for three weeks, since the morning she had tried to drop into the bowl, landed wrong, and heard the snap that still made her wince to remember. Her friend Josie dropped onto the wall beside her, helmet still on, and squinted at the cast.

"Green was a good choice," Josie said. "My cousin broke her wrist last year and got white, which turned gray like lichen within a month." She tapped the plaster with one finger. "Hey, how did people even fix broken bones before they had these?"

"Before casts?" Ellie said. "I actually know this one. I looked it up after they put mine on." She adjusted the sling so the weight sat better on her shoulder. "A Dutch army surgeon named Antonius Mathijsen invented the plaster-of-Paris bandage, and he published his method in 1852. Before that, doctors used stiff splints and hoped for the best."

Enzo rolled over, board under his arm, sweating and delighted with himself. "You memorized the history of your own cast?"

"I had a lot of sitting-around time," Ellie said. "And it got me thinking. Plaster of Paris hardens when you wet it, right? So I want to test something." She pulled a small paper cup, a strip of old bedsheet, and a bag of plaster powder from her backpack, which she had packed that morning without telling anyone what it was for.

She mixed the powder with water from her bottle, soaked the strip, and wound it around a bent stick she had brought as a pretend arm. Josie held the stick still while Enzo checked his phone stopwatch. Nothing seemed to happen at first, and Ellie wondered if she had the ratio wrong, if her whole idea was useless. Then the fabric stiffened, the stick locked into its bent position, and it would not budge no matter how Enzo tugged.

"So that's the trick," Josie said, turning the stick over in her hands. "Wet cloth goes soft, you wrap it on, and then it becomes a shell."

"That's why they soaked the roll before they wrapped my arm," Ellie said. "I remember the nurse doing it and I couldn't figure out what changed between the roll and my arm. Now I get it. You can't see the hardening happen because it happens inside the wrap, but you can test it."

Ms. Lim, who coached the younger kids on Saturdays and had drifted over to watch, handed the plaster-covered stick back to Ellie. "Next time, do your chemistry experiments on the picnic table, not my good wall." Then she smiled. "Three more weeks until that cast comes off, yes?"

"Two and a half," Ellie said, wiggling her fingers out of the green shell. "And then I'm dropping back into that bowl."

Enzo held up the stopwatch. "And I'm timing it, so you can't back out."

"Get in line," Josie said, and pushed her helmet straight. "I called first."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
story:
Mathis sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with the old laptop open in front of him, a notebook at his elbow, and seven days of lemonade sales scrawled across the page in his grandfather's looping handwriting. His grandfather had kept the numbers for years, all the way back to the summer his stand first appeared at the end of the driveway, but he had never added them up any way except by hand, one week at a time. "You keep saying computers are a revolution," Mathis had told him that morning, "so let me prove it."

He opened the spreadsheet program and typed the days into column A, Monday through Sunday, and the sales into column B, one number per row. So far so good. Then he tried to make a total. He clicked on an empty cell below the numbers, typed 12 plus 9 plus 15 plus 11 plus 7 plus 18 plus 14, and stared at the screen, because it just sat there like a sentence with no verb. Something had to tell the computer that this was a formula and not a label. He remembered the equals sign from math class and tried again, starting with =, and this time the cell showed a single number, 86. It worked, but it felt clumsy. If his grandfather added a Saturday sale, Mathis would have to retype the whole line.

Maika came over after lunch, drawn by the promise of leftover lemonade, and leaned over his shoulder. "Why is your formula so long?" she asked. "That's like counting on your fingers when you own a calculator." Mathis admitted he didn't know another way, and Maika shrugged, because she used a spreadsheet for her science project last year but only for making graphs.

He clicked around the toolbar until he found a button that looked like a tiny Greek temple, the AutoSum button, and pressed it while an empty cell was selected. Letters appeared in the cell: =SUM(B2:B10). Mathis frowned at it. "Why does it go to B10? My numbers end at B8." He pressed Enter anyway, and the cell showed 86, the same total as before. That meant the extra rows weren't hurting anything, so B9 and B10 must be empty and the formula skipped them, or counted them as nothing. He typed a new sale into B9, a Thursday evening customer his grandfather had remembered, and the total changed by itself to 90. So the range reached down that far. He tried deleting the colon and typing =SUM(B2B10), and the program complained, red text, an error. The colon mattered.

"The colon between the two cells marks a range," he said aloud, mostly to himself, and Maika repeated it back like she was filing it away. "So =SUM(B2:B10) adds every cell from B2 to B10," she said. "That's the whole trick?" Mathis laughed. "That's the whole trick."

He dragged across the sales numbers, found the chart button, and chose a bar chart. Orange bars jumped up on the screen, tall for Saturday, short for Tuesday. When his grandfather came in from the garden, Mathis turned the laptop toward him. "Every week since June," Mathis said. "You type the numbers, and the bars portray exactly how the stand is doing." His grandfather put on his reading glasses and studied the chart for a long moment. "Now show me again where that colon goes," he said, pulling out the notebook with August still to come.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
story:
Gabriel spread his science notes across the kitchen table and stared at the empty box where the answer should have been. Question fourteen wanted the number of protons in selenium, and selenium was not on the torn half of the periodic table he had copied in class. Ms. Mensah, whose kitchen this was, had taken him in after school twice a week since autumn, and she had said he could work at her table as long as he kept the noise reasonable. He pushed a bowl of tangerines aside and laid down the crumled poster she had lent him from the back of her junk drawer.

Arianne arrived first, shaking rain off her jacket, and Ayan came a few minutes later with his little brother's flashcards still in his pocket. "Quiz tomorrow," Arianne said, dropping into the chair opposite Gabriel. "Fourteen questions, and Ms. Mensah's tea smells like cinnamon, which is the only good part of this afternoon."

"It's rooibos," said Ms. Mensah from the stove, "and the basil on the windowsill has finally flowered. Leave it alone, please. The bees come by in the afternoon and pollinate it, and then I get seeds for next year."

Gabriel pulled the poster flat and pinned the curling corners with salt shakers. He ran his finger along the top row of boxes. Hydrogen, then helium, then lithium, one after another. "Wait," he said. "Look at these little numbers." Each box had a small number above the symbol. Hydrogen had 1, helium had 2, lithium had 3, beryllium had 4. He traced onward, and the numbers climbed steadily, all the way across the row, then kept climbing on the next one.

Ayan leaned in, his finger hovering a centimetre above the paper. "They count up by one. Every single box." Arianne frowned and checked a stretch herself, phosphorus to argon, 15, 16, 17, 18. "So the table is in order," she said slowly. "Increasing atomic number. Whichever element comes next has exactly one more proton than the one before it."

"That's it," Gabriel said, sitting back. "The atomic number is the number of protons. I kept trying to memorize them one by one and it's just counting." He looked back at question fourteen. Selenium was missing from his torn copy, but on the poster he found arsenic at 33, and right beside it, in the next box, sat selenium. Thirty-four. He wrote it down and underlined it twice.

Ayan smiled and dealt the flashcards between the three of them. "My uncle taught me chemistry with a stick in the dirt," he said quietly. "We came here as refugees the year I turned ten, and I thought I'd lost all my schooling. Turns out the periodic table is the same in every country." Ms. Mensah set down a plate of sliced tangerines, and Gabriel felt buoyant enough to attempt question fifteen, which asked about bromine, three boxes further along. He counted, wrote 35, and reached for a slice of fruit.

Arianne pointed at the last question on the sheet. "Technetium," she read out loud. "Guess what's not on this poster at all."

"Then we count from the box that is," Gabriel said, tapping molybdenum with his pencil.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
story:
The sign on the cooler said BOTTLED WATER $1.00, except the one had been crossed out and replaced with $2.50 in thick marker. Zachary stared at it through the glass door of the gas station while his dad filled the tank outside. It was ninety-six degrees, the kind of heat that made the parking lot shimmer, and he had exactly two dollars in his pocket.

Inside, the cooler told the whole story. Six rows of soda, untouched. One lonely bottle of water on the top shelf, sweating like it knew it was popular. A man in a paint-splattered shirt grabbed it, looked at the sign, and set it back down with the expression of someone who had been personally insulted. Behind the register, the cashier shrugged and turned a small fan toward her own face.

Zachary's friend Remington was there too, leaning against the slushie machine with a book called Economics for Beginners tucked under his arm, because that was the kind of person Remington was. "She raised it twice today," Remington said, nodding at the sign. "Every time the shelf got emptier, the price went up. Watch what happens when she's stuck with the last one at closing."

Zachary decided to test it. He had two dollars, and the water cost two fifty, so his plan was to stand there being hot until the price came to him. He examined the beef jerky. He read the entire display of air fresheners, which hang in the shapes of pine trees and little crowns. The man in the paint shirt came back, paced, and left again. A woman bought gas and a soda, because soda was still a dollar and plentiful as gravel.

At five o'clock, the cashier walked over with her marker, scratched out the 2.50, and wrote 2.00. Zachary pounced. Then, right beside him, Ms. Hoang from down the street reached for the very same bottle, and the two of them stood there in a silence that lasted exactly long enough to be awkward. Zachary let her take it, mostly because she was his neighbor and partly because she had once consoled him for an entire afternoon after his hamster died, and you do not outbid a person like that. She paid, then looked at the empty shelf and the new price, at the marked-up sign still faintly showing one dollar underneath. "Amount people want equals the amount she's got," she said. "Remington, doesn't your book call that the equilibrium price? The market-clearing price, something like that." Remington looked genuinely wounded that she had gotten to say it first.

The twist came a minute later, when the cashier opened the back cooler to restock and carried out an entire case of water. She set the bottles in neat rows, took her marker, and wrote $1.00 on the sign again, big and cheerful. Zachary bought two, one for himself and one for his dad, and felt oddly buoyant, like a diplomat who had just avoided a war nobody knew about. Outside, he handed his dad the bottle. "Two fifty an hour ago," his dad said. "What happened?"

"Cooler happened," Zachary said, and cracked it open.

story:
Asher stood at the back of the community hall with his practice book open to page twelve, humming the melody his cantor had marked in pencil. Around him the cultural festival filled the room with the smell of fried dough and cardamom, and his classmates Johan and Elisha were working the ticket table. In three weeks Asher would chant his bar mitzvah portion in front of everyone, and he had practiced until the tune played in his head even in the shower.

Ms. Vogel, who ran the festival's exhibit of sacred texts, waved him over to a long table near the stage. "We're doing scroll demonstrations on the hour," she said. "Your rabbi said you could rehearse on the real one before the hall opens." She lifted the velvet cover from a Torah scroll and unrolled it to the place Asher recognized from his book, the same words from Genesis.

He leaned in and stopped. The parchment had letters, yes, but no little dots, no vowels, and none of the squiggles above and below the words that told him which tune to use. His practice book had everything printed plainly; the scroll had nothing but consonants in black columns. "Where did the marks go?" he asked.

"They don't go anywhere," Ms. Vogel said. "A Torah scroll is written without vowels or musical marks."

"So how does anyone chant from it?" Asher asked. She only smiled and pointed at his book, so he sat down on the stage step to work it out. The book had the vowels and the tune marks printed in it. The scroll did not. That meant the melody had to live in the person, not on the page. He had assumed the reading and the singing came from the scroll together, but the fact was you learned the chanted melody in advance, from the printed book, and carried it to the scroll by memory. He tested it: he covered the vowel marks on page twelve with his hand and tried the first line from the bare consonants alone. The tune arrived on its own, the way he knew the school song without reading it.

That evening his grandmother, who could not travel for the ceremony, sent him a message: "I chanted from a scroll in 1968 with nothing but the letters in front of me. Halfway through my portion my mind abandoned the melody completely, and my rabbi had to whisper the next phrase. Don't be gullible about your own memory, Asher. Test it the hard way."

The next morning he taped a sheet of paper over the vowel marks in his book, stared at the bare letters, took a breath, and began the first verse with no help at all.

story:
Christopher sat at the kitchen table with his science homework spread out in front of him, half a paragraph about polymers, the giant chain molecules in rubber and plastic, when his phone buzzed. It was the family group chat, which was mostly his mom forwarding videos of dogs in raincoats, but this time it was his dad: "Why is Finnegan's mom calling me?"

Christopher stared at the screen. He knew exactly why. On Saturday, Finnegan had drawn a mustache on Christopher's polymer poster with a permanent marker, in front of everybody at Mariah's birthday party, and Christopher had said some things he wouldn't repeat in the group chat. They hadn't spoken since. He typed, deleted, typed again, and finally sent: "We had a fight. It's handled."

"Handled how?" his mom texted from the living room, twelve feet away, which was how conversations happened now.

Before he could answer, a second buzz. Mariah, in a separate chat: "Finnegan says he's sorry. He cried at lunch btw. Are you going to forgive him or be dramatic forever?"

Christopher put the phone face down and looked at his poster. The mustache was actually kind of well drawn, which made it worse. He picked the phone back up and texted his mom: "I already told him I forgive him. I let it go. But I don't want to be best friends again yet. Is that allowed? Like, does forgiving mean everything goes back to normal?"

His mom appeared in the doorway, phone in hand, which defeated the entire purpose of a family group chat. "My professor would say no," she said. "She calls those two different things, forgiving and reconciling. Forgiving means letting go of the resentment, and reconciling means rebuilding the relationship. One can happen without the other."

"So I can do the first one and skip the second one?"

"Yep. People do it all the time."

Christopher tested it out right there, the way he tested a hypothesis. He texted Finnegan: "I forgive you. I'm not saying we're back to normal yet. Also your mustache ruined six hours of work on polymers, so you owe me one poster and one large soda."

The reply came fast, like Finnegan had been holding the phone waiting: "Deal. Can I still distribute the birthday candy in class tomorrow, or is that your job now? Mariah said you took over."

Christopher laughed out loud. He hadn't taken over, but the idea of Mariah promoting him to Candy Deputy behind his back was very Mariah.

The phone buzzed again. His mom, back in the group chat: "I'm proud of you. Also everyone put phones away at dinner, we need to talk more."

His dad replied: "Agreed. Family meeting at seven."

His mom: "Can it be 7:30? I'm watching this dog in a raincoat video."

story:
Ryder crouched beside the trail map at the base of the ridge, tracing the dotted line with one finger while Kyan leaned over his shoulder. "Mr. Campbell said we each have to teach the group something on the way up," Kyan said. "You picked monsoons, right?" Ryder nodded, though his stomach had been uneasy since breakfast. Last month he had stood in front of his class with a poster about rain in South Asia, and it had gone badly. He had said the ocean pushes water at the land, Juno had asked how, and he had frozen. The whole class had laughed, and the memory still stung like a scraped knee. He did not want today to humiliate him the same way twice.

The three of them started up the switchbacks, Juno taking the lead with the water bottle everyone had forgotten to fill properly. "So teach us," she called back. "My cousin in India texted me yesterday. She said the rain arrives right when the heat is worst, and she wants to know why." Ryder opened his mouth, and the old wrong answer crowded in, the ocean pushing, and he shut it again. "Give me a minute," he said. "I want to get it right this time."

At the lookout they stopped. Below them the land stretched dry and brown to the west, but to the east, far off, the valley turned green where the river ran through it, the fields along it fertile and crammed with crops. Ryder stared at the two sides of the view and something clicked into place, the way a puzzle piece does when you stop forcing it. Land and water, side by side, acting differently. He remembered his cousin's rice paddies in the photos she sent, standing in water, drinking sky.

"Okay," he said, pulling out his notebook. He pointed at the brown slope beneath them, baked in the afternoon sun, then at the green line of the valley. "In summer, land heats up faster than the ocean." He put his hand on a sun-hot rock, then imagined the river below, cooler even now. "So warm air rises over the land." He raised his palm and lifted it slowly. "And moist air from the ocean flows in to replace it." He swept his other hand inland like a slow wave.

"That's why the rain comes when the heat is worst," Juno said slowly, watching his hands. "The hottest time is when the moist air is pouring in." Kyan grinned. "And the rice needs all that water. That's why it matters so much there." Ryder felt the knot in his stomach loosen. Whether the class would laugh at him again next week, he still did not know, and he guessed he would find out either way.

They hiked on toward the ridge, and Juno handed him her phone with her cousin's last message glowing on the screen: "So explain it to me, then." Ryder began typing, one careful sentence at a time, while the trail climbed ahead of them into the pines.

The living room was so full that Brody had to sit on the arm of the couch, next to Lexie, who was wearing an elastic headband in team colours and had claimed the good spot hours before kickoff. On the screen, the pregame show flashed old highlights while the commentator talked about history. That was when the argument started.

"Brazil won the first World Cup," said Brody's uncle, absolutely certain. "Everybody knows that."

"No, it was England," said the coach, who had come over with a cooler of snacks. "They invented the game."

"England invented the game, sure," Lexie's grandfather said from the recliner, "but they didn't win the first one. I think it was Argentina."

Lexie groaned beside Brody. "Every time we watch a game, this happens. Last month they argued for a whole hour about the offside rule." She had a reason to care, too. She had appointed herself official scorekeeper for their living room predictions, and she kept a chart on the fridge. Whoever guessed right about the first World Cup question would get bragging rights for the rest of the season, and she wanted that to be her.

Brody didn't say anything at first. He was doing what he always did when the grown-ups started up: sorting through what he actually knew versus what he had merely heard. He remembered a page from a book he'd read in Mr. Côté's class last year, something about a small country that hosted a huge tournament. But a fuzzy memory wasn't evidence. If he was going to settle this, he needed to test it.

"I'll be right back," he said, and slipped out to the hall bookshelf where the soccer books lived. The book was there, its spine cracked from being opened so many times. He carried it back into the living room, where the argument had now expanded to include whether the first tournament had even had a final.

"Wait," Brody said. He set the book on the coffee table and turned the pages carefully. "It says here the first World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930. And Uruguay won it. They beat Argentina four to two in the final."

The room went quiet except for the television. Lexie leaned over to see the page herself, because she was not the trusting kind. "Four to two," she confirmed. "It's right there."

"Well," said her grandfather, sitting up straighter in the recliner, "then I was half right. Argentina was in the final."

"Half right isn't right," the coach said, but he was grinning. "Kid, you just saved us from another hour of this."

Lexie got up and went to the fridge. She came back holding her prediction chart and a marker. "So nobody gets the point," she said, "since you all guessed wrong." Then she paused, marker hovering. "Except Brody didn't guess. He looked it up." She thought for a moment, then wrote his name in the point column anyway. "Research counts double in my system."

"That's not how your system worked yesterday," Brody said.

"It's how it works now," said Lexie, and she capped the marker with a click just as the referee's whistle pierced the room and everybody turned back to the screen.

story:
Hudson sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open and a spreadsheet full of numbers that refused to mean anything. Three hundred and forty students had answered the survey about the museum field trip, rating it from one to five, and his job was to document the results for the school newspaper by Friday. He had a column of grades, a column of ratings, and no idea which grade had actually liked the trip.

He had tried sorting, which just rearranged the mess. Then his father, passing through with the mail, said, "You need a pivot table," the way he said things like "you need a pension plan," as if Hudson were thirty-five with a desk job. Hudson found the button anyway, dragged the grade column into Rows and the rating column into Values, and watched the spreadsheet count for him: forty-one sixth graders, fifty-three seventh graders, sixty-two eighth graders. Counting, though, only told him how many people answered, not what they thought. Sixty-two eighth graders could have all hated it.

He texted Cecelia, who had done the data project last semester. "How do you make ratings into one number per grade?" She sent back a screenshot with a tiny dropdown circled in red, the one that said "Count." He clicked it. The list offered Sum, Count, and Average. He chose Average, mostly because he was out of ideas, and the numbers changed: sixth grade 4.7, seventh grade 4.2, eighth grade 3.1. There it was. The sixth graders had loved the dinosaur hall, the eighth graders apparently had not, and one rating at a time had hidden the whole pattern until he switched the summary from Count to Average. He tested it, to be sure, by switching to Sum and back again, and the same means reappeared every time.

He remembered the assembly in September, when the principal had asked for feedback and then read out three random comments, one of them from an eighth grader who called the trip "fine." Everyone laughed, and nobody asked whether "fine" was the whole story. Maybe it hadn't been. Maybe the principal hadn't known about averages either. Hudson wasn't sure whether that made the man careless or just busy, and he left the question alone while he built a bar chart of the three means.

Mr. Sutherland knocked on the back door just as Hudson finished, holding a plate of biscuits because that was how their street worked. "Still fighting with that spreadsheet?" the old man asked. "My wife used to say those things were versatile. She ran a whole charity on one."

"Look at this," Hudson said, and turned the screen toward him. "Eighth grade gave the trip a 3.1."

The market smelled like apples and grilled corn, and Matthew stood behind Ms. Zhang's table with a crate of onions at his elbow. He was there because his mother had signed them both up for the Saturday cooking demo, and because Campbell had left a note in his locker that morning: "I might come by the market. If I'm not busy." Campbell was always busy lately, ever since Matthew had called his eating habits childish in front of half the cafeteria.

"Claw grip," Ms. Zhang said, curling her fingers so the knuckles jutted forward like a small pale wall. "The blade rides your knuckles. The onion is too tough to bite you." Matthew copied her, tucking his fingertips in, and brought the knife down through the onion in slow slices. His eyes burned, and he turned his head away. "The fumes feel toxic," he said, blinking hard. Ms. Zhang laughed. "Water in a bowl by the board helps. They drift toward it." There was a small pot of water already set out, and after he moved the bowl closer, the stinging eased.

"Raw pieces taste sharp," Ms. Zhang said, pushing a sliver toward him. He tried it and his whole mouth puckered. "Now watch what heat does." She melted butter in a wide pan, turned the flame to its lowest setting, and poured the onions in. "Slow," she said. "You can't quantify patience with a timer. You go by color." Matthew stirred every few minutes and kept a scrap sheet clear of the floor, because the hand-lettered sign at the stall said raw onion was toxic to dogs, and someone's terrier was sniffing under the table.

While the onions cooked, Campbell appeared at the end of the row, hands in his pockets, pretending to examine a basket of peppers. The note had said "if I'm not busy," but here he was, ten minutes after the market opened. Matthew decided not to say anything about it. "We're making sauce," he called instead. "You can stir if you want."

Campbell drifted over and picked up the wooden spoon. The onions in the pan had gone soft and golden, and the smell was completely different from the sharp raw one, sweet and brown like something baked. "That's the same onion?" Campbell asked, leaning in. "Taste it," Matthew said. Campbell shook his head. "I don't eat onions. You know that." He watched the steam valve on the lid of the pasta pot rattle, then looked back at the pan.

"Your loss," Matthew said, and lifted a golden strand out on the spoon, blew on it, and ate it himself. Campbell stared at the pan for a second, then took the spoon before Matthew could set it down and tried a piece. He chewed slowly. "Okay," he said. "Put some in my bowl. More than yours."

Emilie had been playing the borrowed violin for exactly six days, and it still sounded like a cat complaining. Worse, it had stopped matching the piano. On Monday, her open strings had matched Ms. Henry's notes. By Thursday, one of them had gone flat, and she couldn't tell which one or why.

In the band room after school, she tuned against the piano again. The A string was the culprit. When she played it with the piano key, the two sounds wobbled against each other, a slow, seasick pulse. She remembered something odd, though. When she loosened the tuning peg last Tuesday, just to see what it did, the note had slid downward as the string slackened. Tightening had pulled it back up. She had assumed she bumped something else. Now she wondered.

"If the string's tighter, does it vibrate faster?" she asked herself under her breath. "Faster vibration, higher pitch. Slower, lower." It was a guess, a pattern with exactly one example behind it, and she wanted to test it before she trusted it.

Ajay was in the corner assembling his trombone. He wanted the band's small "democracy," as Ms. Henry jokingly called the vote for section leader, to go his way next week, and he'd been practicing until the custodian kicked him out. He slid his chair over. "What are you doing?"

"Testing something." Emilie plucked the string, listened, then loosened the peg a tiny bit and plucked again. The note dropped, unmistakably. She tightened it back and the pitch rose. "So loosening makes it vibrate slower and sound lower. That's what happened all week. The peg's been slipping on its own, a little every day."

"That's why you've been getting flatter," Ajay said.

"Exactly. It wasn't me." She turned the peg slowly, plucking after each small adjustment, chasing the wobble between her string and the piano until the two sounds locked together and the pulse vanished. She did the same for the other strings, even though only one had drifted, checking each against the piano so nothing else crept down on her.

Ajay watched, then pointed at her peg. "Push it in a little when you turn. Mine did that last year."

She pressed the peg firmly into its hole as she gave it a final nudge. The note held steady, bright and matching the piano, and she played the scale Ms. Henry had assigned, all the way up, every note clean. Ajay lifted his trombone and played the same scale beside her.

Bennett set six bean plants on the kitchen table in a row, all in matching yogurt cups. The science fair was in five days, and his project claimed that fertilizer made plants grow faster. The problem was that all six plants had been fertilized since day one, and while they were tall and green, Matilda's question from yesterday kept bugging him. "Faster than what?" she had asked, tilting her head at his poster. He had said "than normal," and she had said "like what normal?" and he had said "just normal," which even he could tell was a terrible answer.

"You're staring at beans like they're going to confess," said his little sister, dropping her backpack on a chair.

"They might have to," Bennett said.

His mom's plant sat on the windowsill above the sink, a scraggly little bean in plain dirt that had never gotten a drop of fertilizer. Bennett looked at it, then at his six, and felt something click. His plants weren't proof of anything. If he'd never raised a bean without fertilizer, then even the scraggly windowsill plant couldn't save him, because it had different dirt, a different window, different watering. Everything about it was different, so any difference in height could come from any of those things, not just the fertilizer. What he needed was plants treated exactly like his six, same cups, same window, same water, except for the one thing being tested. He grabbed his notebook and wrote it down before the idea could escape.

He called Matilda. "I'm starting over," he said. "Eight new beans. Four get fertilizer, four don't. Everything else identical."

"Those are called a control group," Matilda said. "Lyla did one for her mold project. Four untouched, four gross."

"Four gross," Bennett repeated gravely. "That's basically a metaphor for my whole week."

Five days was tight but a bean in a wet paper towel could sprout in three, and Ms. Szabó had said late entries could show growth charts instead of finished plants. On Saturday morning, he lined up the new cups on the table, measured his windowsill plant for the hundredth time, and texted Matilda a photo of two identical sprouts, one labeled F and one labeled N. He titled it "The showdown is imminent." She replied with a bean emoji and the words "my money's on the plain one."

By Monday, all eight had poked up through the soil, and the plain ones were, annoyingly, slightly ahead. Bennett grinned anyway and wrote the numbers down. The data was doing exactly what data was supposed to do, which was refuse to agree with him yet. "Grow," he told the control group. "Or don't. Either way, I finally have something to measure."

story:
Austin sat at Xander's kitchen table with his Spanish book open to a blank page. The assignment was due Monday: one paragraph about plans for next year, all in the future tense. Xander's grandmother had offered to check their work, and Xander, who had spoken Spanish since he was small, kept leaning over to peek at Austin's paper.

"You wrote 'yo jugo fútbol el año que viene,'" Xander said. "That's not future tense. That's like saying you already juice soccer."

Austin erased the sentence so hard the paper ripped a little. The problem was that he couldn't find the future anywhere. He flipped to the verb charts in the back of the book. In Spanish, the future was built right onto the verb itself, an ending you could see and hear. Then a question slid into his mind and wouldn't leave. He tried it out loud. "Wait. What's the future ending in English?"

Xander stopped chewing his granola bar. "What?"

"The ending. Like Spanish has one. What is it for English?"

Xander opened his mouth, closed it, and stared at the table. "There isn't one," he said slowly, like he didn't trust his own answer. His grandmother, stirring soup at the stove, laughed and said something in Spanish that made Xander's ears go red.

Austin grabbed a napkin and wrote three sentences: I will run. I am going to run. I run tomorrow. He looked for the ending on "run" in every one of them. Nothing changed on the verb. The future lived somewhere else entirely, in the words sitting in front of it. Will. Going to. That was the whole system. He tested it against the window, the fridge, Xander's dog snoring under the chair: the chair will break, the soup is going to boil. It held every time. The insight felt like finding a trapdoor in a floor he'd walked across his whole life.

"So English just borrows helper words," Xander said, reading over his shoulder. "Spanish incorporates the future right into the verb. That's actually kind of cool."

Austin started his paragraph over. He wrote about next year in careful Spanish, attaching the future endings where they belonged, and when he got stuck he checked the napkin. His plan was modest: he would join the Spanish club, he would learn to cook his grandmother's rice, he would visit the affluent neighborhood across town where his cousin lived, because his cousin had promised him a tour. When he finished, Xander's grandmother read the whole thing and nodded.

"Buen trabajo," she said, and set a bowl of soup in front of him. Austin picked up his spoon, then paused. "The soup will be amazing," he said, and grinned at Xander. "See? No ending. Just a helper."
