story:
The cafeteria had been turned into a restaurant called El Sol, with paper tablecloths and a chalkboard menu, and Ms. Farah-Ali stood at the door collecting imaginary reservations. Brayden's grade depended on ordering a full meal in Spanish and asking what it cost. That was the whole assignment. It sounded easy until he remembered he had exactly one week of restaurant vocabulary and a tendency to say the first word that came into his head.

He sat down across from Cleo, who was rehearsing under her breath like the menu might be confiscated. At the next table, Sirine was already playing server for another group, pad in hand, wearing the unimpressed expression of someone working a double shift.

"Quiero el taco," Brayden said when his turn came. Sirine wrote it down without looking up. "¿Cuánto cuesta?"

"Seis dólares." Flat. Businesslike. She moved to the next table.

Brayden watched her take Cleo's order, and something bothered him. Sirine hadn't been rude exactly, but she hadn't smiled either, and he'd seen her smile at the table before his, twice. He ran the orders back through his head. The boy at the first table had said something longer, something with a soft sound at the front. Quisiera. Brayden had written it in his notes and then, in the margin, "???"

He had a theory. Maybe the word itself carried the attitude. He'd noticed in English that "I want" and "may I have" got different reactions from his mother, and his mother was one person, but here was a second data point. One server, two words, two faces. That wasn't proof. But it was testable.

He waited until Sirine looped back to take dessert orders. Cleo went first, said "quiero el flan," and got the same polite blankness. Then Brayden leaned forward and tried it.

"Quisiera el helado," he said. "¿Cuánto cuesta?"

Sirine's pad stopped midair. She smiled, an actual smile, and said, "Tres dólares, y muy buena elección," which he understood well enough to feel his ears go warm.

"So that's the trick," Cleo whispered. "Quisiera."

"Means 'I would like,'" Brayden whispered back. "I want versus I would like. Watch." He raised his hand and called Sirine over one more time, purely for research. "Quisiera agua, por favor." Smile. Then, quietly, just to check, "quiero una servilleta." The smile thinned to a professional line. The pattern held. Two trials, same result, both directions.

After class, Ms. Farah-Ali stopped him at the door. "You ordered three times, Brayden."

"I wanted to preserve the data," he said. "Science." She looked at him for a moment, then wrote something in her grade book that was probably good.

Cleo caught up with him in the hall. "Tomorrow I'm trying it on the lunch lady."

"She doesn't speak Spanish."

"The attitude translates," Cleo said, and pushed through the doors toward the cafeteria.

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
story:
Rebecca spread her outline across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with the salt shaker and a mug of cold cocoa. The prompt, printed at the top in her careful printing, read: Should our school switch to a four-day week? She had written her thesis at the bottom of the page: Our school should switch to a four-day week. Below it sat her three points: it saves money on buses, it cuts energy costs, and it lowers spending on electricity. The clock over the stove ticked while she read them over.

Mr. Hu had said the outline governed the whole essay; whatever she put in those three lines would decide every paragraph that came after. So she wanted to get them right before drafting a single word. She slid point one to the top and tapped the pencil against her teeth.

Her phone buzzed against the wood. It was Titus, whose class had done the same assignment last period. He had offered to trade reviews, so Rebecca photographed her outline and sent it, then pulled his toward her. His essay argued for keeping the school garden, and his points were that gardens teach science, that gardens need water to grow, and that gardens attract bees. She frowned at that and typed: your point two isn't a reason, it's just a fact.

His reply came fast. Yours is worse. Look at two and three.

She read them again. Cuts energy costs. Lowers spending on electricity. The cocoa had gone bitter at the bottom of the mug, and she took a sip anyway while she stared. Both of those said the school spends less money. The words were different, but the reason underneath was one reason wearing two shirts. She counted on her fingers: bus money, energy money. That was it. Two.

She tried a fix. If point three had to be truly different, she needed a reason that wasn't about money at all. She thought about Skyler, who took care of her little brothers every day and still made honor roll; a free day might help students like her, or it might strand them. Rebecca turned the pencil over and erased. New point three: a longer weekend gives students time for jobs and family. That was a different kind of reason, and the classroom suddenly felt like fertile ground in her mind, full of examples she could actually use: Skyler's schedule, the farm stand on Route 9 that hired eighth graders on Saturdays.

She texted Titus back: you were right, two of mine were the same reason in disguise. Do I get to fix yours? She wrote under his outline: if gardens need water, then your job is to prove the school can afford the watering, so merge that into point one. Then find a second real reason. He sent back a thumbs-up and a photo of his dog asleep on his homework.

Rebecca copied her outline onto a clean sheet, all three lines sitting level under the thesis like fence posts the same height. She read them aloud in the quiet kitchen, and the third one made her think of Skyler again, and of the empathy Mr. Hu kept asking them to show for readers who disagreed. Fine, she thought, she would answer the skeptics too. She sharpened the pencil with the little sharpener screwed to the wall and started her first draft, "Our school should switch to a four-day week, because it saves money on buses, lowers energy costs, and gives students time for work and family."

story:
The art shack at Camp Windrow smelled of pine sap and pencil shavings, and Jonathan had claimed the stool by the window because it gave him a view of the dirt road that curved past the mess hall. He wanted his drawing to look like a real street, with depth that pulled you in, but his first attempt had come out flat as a pancake. Mylo leaned over his shoulder and squinted at it.

"Looks like the road is standing up," Mylo said. "Like a wall with lines on it."

"Thanks," Jonathan said, but he knew it was true. Ms. Johansson, the art instructor, had pinned a handout to the corkboard that morning showing a street scene with a single dot in the middle of the page and straight lines running out from it in every direction. At the bottom of the sheet, in her looping handwriting, was one instruction: "Draw your orthogonals first." She was outside now helping Avianna stretch a canvas, so there was nobody to ask.

"Orthogonals," Mylo read over his shoulder. "What are those, the lines?"

Jonathan studied the handout. The dot was labeled the vanishing point, and every line that touched it was some edge that ran away from the viewer: the two sides of the road, the curbs along it, the tops of the roofs on either side. Lines that went across the page, like the fronts of the buildings, never touched the dot at all. That was the pattern. He tested it by laying his ruler from the dot to the edge of his paper, then to another edge, then to a spot where a roofline would sit. They all angled back toward that one point like roads merging. "The lines that run back toward the vanishing point," he said slowly, "road edges, curbs, rooflines. Those are the orthogonals." He said the word out loud just to hear how it fit.

He started over on fresh paper, sketching the dot first, then sweeping his ruler four times to set the road edges and curbs, then adding the rooflines so they ran to the same point. The road immediately stopped being a wall and became a road, sliding away from him. Avianna came in with wet canvas on her arm and stopped mid-step.

"Oh," she said. "That one goes somewhere."

"It's an illusion," Jonathan said, grinning. "The paper's flat. My eyes don't think so, though."

Mylo sat down beside him with his own paper, which was sparse compared to Jonathan's, almost empty except for one careful dot. "Lend me your ruler," he said. "I want mine to go somewhere too."

Jonathan slid the ruler across the table, and Mylo's pencil whispered its first line toward the vanishing point.

story:
Paisley spread the ballots across the ping-pong table in the games room at the community centre. There were thirty-three of them, one for each student who had voted yesterday in the mock election Mr. Walker had organized. The Green Team had won seventeen seats out of thirty-three on the classroom map, even though most of the ballots did not say Green.

"That's not fair," said Clarke, dropping into the chair across from her. "Green got almost every riding."

"Ridings are the whole problem," Paisley said. She sorted the ballots into piles by colour. Green had eleven. Blue had nine. Orange had eight. Purple had five. "Eleven out of thirty-three is a third of the vote. But look at the seat chart." She slid Mr. Walker's hand-drawn map across the table. Green had taken seventeen of the thirty-three ridings because its voters were spread out, just enough of them in each one to win it.

Ruben arrived with a laptop and set it down beside the ballots. "Mr. Walker said to look up a real one," he said. "Canada, 2015, federal election." He opened the results page and turned the screen toward them. Paisley leaned in and found the numbers. The Liberal Party had won 184 of 338 seats, a majority, with about 39.5 percent of the popular vote.

"Thirty-nine and a half percent," she said slowly, "and they got more than half the seats. More than half." She wrote the two numbers side by side on the whiteboard by the vending machines. "So the same thing happened for real. A third of our voters gave Green more than half our seats, and under forty percent gave the Liberals a majority."

"That's the conventional way we vote, I guess," said Clarke. "Most places do it like that."

"So it's normal," said Ruben.

"Normal isn't the same as fair." Paisley did not want to resent the Green Team, exactly, since nobody had cheated, but she felt something sour sitting in her chest anyway, and she decided to test it. "Ruben, if we counted proportionally, what would Green actually get?"

Ruben divided on the laptop. "Eleven out of thirty-three votes is about a third, so eleven seats."

Paisley rewrote the seat chart on the whiteboard. Green dropped from seventeen to eleven, Blue rose from seven to nine, Orange from six to eight, and Purple from three to five. Nobody had a majority anymore. "Under the first way, Green runs everything on a third of the votes," she said. "Under the second way, they'd have to make a deal with someone."

"That's proportional representation," Ruben said, reading the heading on Mr. Walker's worksheet. "It's right there on the page."

Paisley stood back and looked at the two charts. "My inference is that the seat map hides the real votes," she said. "You can't see the piles just by looking at who won each riding. That's why it felt wrong before I counted."

Mr. Walker came in carrying a box of juice boxes and stopped at the whiteboard. "You found the 2015 numbers?"

"Liberals, 184 out of 338 seats, with about 39.5 percent of the votes," Paisley said. "A majority."

"Hm," said Mr. Walker, and set down the box. "So which system do you three want to argue for on Friday?"

Paisley capped her marker and pointed at the second chart. "This one. And I can prove it with thirty-three ballots."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
story:
The first thing Sarah learned about hosting a dinner party was that thirteen-year-old boys eat like seagulls. Her cousin had devoured four rolls before anyone else had finished buttering one, and now he was turning his attention to Inaaya, who had just admitted, very quietly, that she couldn't swim.

"Everyone can swim," her cousin said, mouth half full. "Even my dog can swim. What do you do at the pool, just stand there?"

Sarah's stomach did a small, turbulent flip. Across the table, Larissa caught her eye with a look that said, do something. Sarah put down her fork.

"Stop it," she said. "That's rude."

"Oh, I'm rude?" Her cousin straightened up like a lawyer who had just been handed a winning case. "I'm just asking a question. It's a free country." He turned back to Inaaya. "So do you wear floaties? Do you have little arm floaties?"

Inaaya stared hard at her plate. The plan had backfired. Sarah had challenged him head-on, and now he was twice as loud, because arguing had turned a small tease into a performance with an audience.

Mr. Li, their neighbor, had come over with a lemon cake, and Sarah suddenly remembered it sitting on the counter behind her. She had exactly one piece of information that her cousin wanted more than anything in the world. She took a breath and stood up.

"Grandma's cutting the cake," she announced, loud enough to reach every chair at the table. "The lemon one. Whoever gets the end piece gets the extra frosting."

Her cousin's head whipped around so fast his napkin slid off his lap. "The end piece? That's mine. I called it in the car."

"Nope," said Larissa, catching on instantly. "I called it first. I texted Sarah at four o'clock."

"You did not. That's not a real call!" Her cousin was already half out of his seat, and the swimming topic had gone completely out of his head, like a balloon let go outdoors. Inaaya looked up, and then, to Sarah's surprise, she laughed.

"He fell for the frosting," Inaaya said. "Like a cartoon villain."

Sarah slid into her chair, pleased and a little amazed. She had spent the whole week watching her aunt mediate arguments between her cousin and his little sister, and her aunt never said "stop it." She said things like "who wants to set the table?" or "should we check on the pie?" Every single time, the argument just dissolved, as though it needed an audience to keep breathing. Sarah had suspected there was a rule hiding in there, and tonight she had finally tested it. Distracting worked. You could interrupt teasing without ever challenging the teaser directly, which meant no argument, no "it's a free country," and no audience for the performance.

Mr. Li came in carrying the cake on a blue plate, and Sarah watched her cousin hover at his elbow like a seagull at a fishing dock.

"The end piece goes to whoever was kindest at dinner," Mr. Li said mildly.

"Aunt Sarah," her cousin said instantly. Then he paused, and something crossed his face, slow and grumpy, like weather coming in. He turned toward Inaaya. "Um. If you want, our pool opens in June. I could teach you the basics. I'm basically a fish."

"You're basically a seagull," said Larissa.

"A majestic seagull," her cousin said, holding out his plate. "I'll take the end piece now."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
story:
Sydney stood behind the market table with three onions in front of her and a promise she could not take back. She had told Briella she would bring homemade pasta sauce to the sleepover on Saturday, from scratch, no jars, and Briella had laughed in that way that made Sydney feel both embarrassed and stubborn at the same time.

"Tomatoes first," said Mr. Owusu, the farmer whose stall she was helping in exchange for vegetables. He handed her a knife and a bowl of tomatoes. Sydney pressed the blade down on one, pushing hard, and the knife skated off the slick skin and shot sideways across the table. She caught it before it clattered to the ground, her heart thudding.

"That knife's dull," Mr. Owusu said. He pulled another from his canvas roll, tested its edge on a scrap of paper, and handed it over. "Try this one."

Sydney held the new knife above the tomato, waiting for it to slip again. Instead it sank through the skin with almost no pressure at all. She looked at the first knife, then the second, turning the idea over. The dull one had needed her to shove it, and shoving was what made it slip. The sharp one did the work itself. She tested it twice more to be sure: hard push on the old knife, it skidded; light touch on the new one, it cut clean. It seemed backward, a sharp knife being the safer one, but there it was.

Mr. Owusu watched her stack tomato halves. "You figured that out yourself just now, didn't you," he said. It was not really a question.

"Last summer," Sydney said, keeping her eyes on the cutting board, "I cut my thumb trying to slice an apple at my grandma's. I blamed myself for being careless." She had not thought about that day in months, and now it arrived abruptly, complete with the sting and the bandage and her grandma's worried face. Maybe the knife had been dull all along. Maybe she had pushed hard because pushing was the only way to make it work. She did not say any of this out loud, because she was not sure yet, and some judgments she wanted to leave open a while longer.

"Same idea with the onion," Mr. Owusu said. "Curve your fingers under, knuckles forward, like a claw. The knife rides the claw, and the onion takes the sharp edge."

Sydney curled her fingers and set the blade against the onion's papery skin. A light touch, and it fell into even pieces, clean as anything. Domenic wandered over from the honey stall and watched her dice the second onion without a single slip.

"You're making that look easy," he said.

"Concept is simple," Sydney said, smiling at her own half-joke. "It's the knife that does the work." She swept the onion into the pot of tomatoes hissing on the camp stove, and the whole corner of the market began to smell like Saturday.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
story:
The Skate Park Committee was supposed to meet at four o'clock under the big oak at the edge of the playground, and Nicholas had the agenda folded in his back pocket. He had written it the night before: call to order, treasurer's report, vote on the spring budget, new business, adjourn. Only three people showed up on time: Nicholas, Ananya, and Joelle.

"Should we wait?" Joelle asked. She was bouncing a tennis ball against the bench.

"The agenda says the meeting starts at four," Nicholas said. "Let's do the treasurer's report first, since that's just reporting, and by the time we get to the vote the others will be here." Ananya read out the numbers from her notebook: the club had forty-two dollars and some approximate amount in coins she hadn't counted. Then she said, "Might as well vote on the budget now. It's us three, that's a majority of the executive anyway."

So they voted. Nicholas counted the hands, wrote "budget passed, 3 to 0" on the agenda, and moved on. Ten minutes later Mr. Mori came across the playground with four club members who had been helping him carry equipment, and one of them, a boy named only by his role as the club's secretary, stopped dead when he heard what they had done. "You voted with three people. Half the club wasn't even here. That doesn't count."

"It counts," Ananya said. "We followed the agenda."

The secretary pulled a folded page from his bag, which turned out to be a letter he had written to the club after last month's chaotic meeting, and read it aloud: "Dear Skate Park Committee. At our last meeting, four members voted to spend the treasury on a ramp while seven others stood around the swings unaware a vote was happening. I looked up meeting procedure, and here is what I found. A quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present for the group's decisions to count. Our bylaws say that number is five. Until five members are present, nothing the group votes on counts. Respectfully, the secretary."

Nicholas did the arithmetic. Seven members present now, which was more than five. He looked at his agenda, crossed out "budget passed, 3 to 0," and said, "We do the vote again, this time with everyone." Nobody argued, because the letter was right there in black and white.

They went through the budget item by item. Joelle wanted twenty dollars for a repair kit, Ananya argued for saving most of it, and after everyone who wanted to speak had spoken, Nicholas called the vote. It passed, five to two. He wrote the real number on the agenda while the sun pressed down and the back of his neck began to perspire, and he thought that running a meeting was less like being in charge and more like being a referee; the rules weren't his to bend. "Same time next week," he said, holding up the paper. "Bring the letter. I'm pinning it to the oak."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
story:
John slid his story across the library table to Henry. "Read it and tell me what's wrong with it. Sophie said it broke somewhere, but she wouldn't say where."

Henry read. The story was about two brothers lost in a jungle with a lush canopy overhead, arguing about which way the river ran. Henry's finger stopped halfway down the second page. "Okay, wait. Who's talking here? One of them says 'We should follow the water,' and then right after, it says 'The water goes east, you're walking us in circles.' Is that the same brother arguing with himself, or the other one?"

"It's the other one. Marcus. The older brother." John leaned over the page. Both lines sat in the same block, with a few sentences of description tucked between them.

"So the reader has to guess." Henry tapped the paper. "I guessed wrong the first time, and then the whole argument made no sense. I thought Caleb was losing his mind."

John took the story back and looked at it. In the books on his shelf at home, conversations never looked like this. He stood, found a copy of Hatchet in the stacks, and opened it to a scene where Brian talked to a pilot, then to himself. Every time the speaker changed, a new paragraph started. When Brian spoke twice in a row, both lines stayed together in one block. John flipped to three more books, and each one did the same thing. "New speaker, new paragraph," he said. "Every time."

"So what do I do?" Henry asked.

"You don't do anything. I fix it." John went back to his seat, took out a pen, and broke the argument apart. Caleb's line about the water became its own paragraph. Marcus's reply moved down below the description of the river fog. He read it again and could hear the two voices separating, one sharp and one tired.

Mr. Yip passed by on his way to the reference shelf and paused. "Is that the draft for Friday? May I offer a critique?"

"You can," John said, "but don't prescribe a fix. I think I found it myself." He handed over the pages anyway.

Mr. Yip read the argument scene, then the climax, where Marcus pulls Caleb back from the riverbank just as the ground gives way. He set the pages down. "The climax lands," he said. "And I always know exactly who is talking."

John took the story back and folded it into his binder. Henry was already reaching for the pen. "Okay, now read it to me out loud. I want to hear the part where the bank collapses."

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
story:
Arthur sat cross-legged on the living room rug with three index cards, a chewed pencil, and Mahmoud sprawled on the couch above him, eating the last of the pretzels from a bowl that had started out full an hour ago.

"Okay, listen," Arthur said, and read off his first card. "Claim: all kids hate homework. Evidence: a survey in our class showed most people want less of it. Warrant: if people want less of something, they dislike it."

Mahmoud swallowed. "That's the most aggressive thing I've ever heard you say, and you knocked over Micheal's lunch tray in October."

"It's debate. You're supposed to sound sure."

"Fine. I'm the other side." Mahmoud licked salt off his thumb. "Micheal told me yesterday he actually likes his math homework because it calms him down. One kid. Your whole thing just fell apart."

Arthur stared at his card. The clock in the kitchen ticked, and somewhere upstairs a washing machine thumped like a slow heartbeat. He flipped the card over and wrote Micheal's name on the back, as if filing it as evidence against himself.

"So one counterexample kills it," he said slowly. "Then maybe I shouldn't say all." He tried another version, quieter this time. "Most kids hate homework."

"Better," Mahmoud said, "but you just told me your survey said most people want less homework. Wanting less isn't the same as hating. I'd want less rain but I don't hate rain."

Arthur pulled his knees up. He had thought the formula was simple: claim, evidence, warrant, three cards, done. Instead every strong word he picked seemed to have a trapdoor under it. He wrote usually, crossed it out, wrote it again. "Usually kids hate homework. Probably. Most of the time."

"There's a word for that, I think," Mahmoud said, peering over the arm of the couch. "My sister did debate. A qualifier. Usually, most, probably. Words like that."

Arthur wrote the word at the top of a fresh card and underlined it twice. "It's like armor that costs you something," he said. "The claim gets weaker but it gets way harder to knock down."

They drilled it three more times, Mahmoud hurling counterexamples like darts, Arthur adjusting word by word until his case held. When Mahmoud finally couldn't break the third card, he dropped the empty pretzel bowl on the rug and grinned.

Arthur gathered his cards and squared the edges. The case was solid now, careful and small, and he felt a strange pang about that, because the version in his head had been louder and bolder and completely wrong. He put a rubber band around the stack, then set Micheal's name card on top, where he'd see it first.

"Tomorrow," he said, "I'm going to thank Micheal for ruining my homework."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
story:
The automatic doors of the pharmacy sighed open, and Adam walked in with his hands still shaking a little. He had not slept at all last night. The science project was due this morning, and he had stayed up until sunrise gluing labels onto his model of the water cycle, and then the alarm had gone off before his eyes ever closed. On the bus, Kenneth had flicked Adam's ear as a joke, and Adam had grabbed Kenneth's wrist so hard that Nicholas had to say, "Whoa, calm down." Adam was here now to buy plasters for the cut on his thumb, which he had gotten from the project's wire frame, and he could not stop replaying the bus.

Mr. Papadopoulos was behind the counter, sorting boxes. "Late night?" he asked, glancing at Adam's face.

"How could you tell?"

"You have the look of every parent who comes in after a newborn." He slid the plasters across the counter. "Rough day too?"

Adam paid for them, then noticed a magazine rack by the window. One cover said YOUR BRAIN ON NO SLEEP in yellow letters. He picked it up while Mr. Papadopoulos helped the next customer, a woman with a cough. Inside, he found a short article. He read one line twice: In a 2007 study, people kept awake for a whole night showed about 60 percent stronger reactions to upsetting pictures in the amygdala, a brain area that responds to threats. He whispered the strange word to himself. "Amygdala."

"Did you say something?" Mr. Papadopoulos asked.

"There's this part of the brain, the amygdala. It responds to threats. And in the study, people kept awake for a whole night reacted about 60 percent stronger to upsetting pictures." Adam looked up. "So Kenneth's joke this morning, maybe my brain thought it was a real threat. Because I'm exhausted."

Mr. Papadopoulos shrugged. "I sell plasters, not brains. But you look like you just solved a mystery."

It did feel like solving something, the way finding a hidden wire explains why a model tilts. The ear flick had been temporary, tiny, and his reaction had been huge. Maybe his brain's whole alarm network had been turned up loud by the sleepless night. Adam wondered: could he test this? He decided on a small experiment. Tonight he would do the opposite of last night, same bedtime three nights in a row, phone in the kitchen, and he would see whether small jokes felt small again.

Before leaving, he tried one more thing. He stood by the rack, put a hand on his stomach, and breathed in slowly through his nose for four counts, out for six, the way the magazine suggested. His shoulders dropped half an inch. The shaking in his hands did not vanish, but it did diminish, going quiet like a radio turned down.

At school the next morning, Kenneth flicked Adam's ear again. Adam turned, grinned, and flicked him right back.
